title: DOJ Launches Antitrust Probe into Major News Networks After White House Boycott
snippet: Federal investigators are looking into whether five major television networks violated antitrust laws by briefly suspending press pool coverage in response to White House credential revocations.
content:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of Justice has opened an antitrust investigation into the nation's primary television news networks following their joint decision to briefly boycott White House press pool coverage, federal officials confirmed Saturday.

The probe targets ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC, and Fox News to determine whether their coordinated stand against the White House violated the Sherman Act, a federal statute prohibiting anticompetitive behavior and group boycotts among commercial rivals. The investigation, first reported by The New York Times, marks a dramatic escalation in the ongoing legal and political friction between the administration and the press corps.

Solidarity Among Competitors

The controversy stems from a mid-September incident in which the White House stripped press credentials from journalists representing CNN, Politico, and MS NOW, declaring that access to the president is a privilege rather than a right. In response, the impacted news outlets filed a First Amendment lawsuit against the administration, alleging unlawful retaliation over critical news coverage.

In a rare show of industry unity, all five major broadcast and cable news networks that comprise the primary White House press pool—including Fox News—refused to send replacement crews, effectively pausing shared press coverage. Under standard pool arrangements, these outlets split operational costs and share video footage with hundreds of local and national media affiliates nationwide.

Legal Battles and Broader Implications

The press blackout was short-lived. On September 24, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the administration to immediately restore the journalists' credentials, ruling that the sudden ban likely violated constitutional protections. Despite the court order, lingering disputes over pool assignments and event access persisted.

Legal experts note that the Justice Department's antitrust inquiry creates unprecedented financial and regulatory pressure on major media companies. By framing collective editorial decisions as potentially illegal collusion, the probe adds a new federal leverage point in the administration's long-running battles with news organizations.
